strap: A daily dispatch from the world you are entering

lead.title: Washington turns the private household into a regulated workplace, and every family with staff there will need written terms
lead.standfirst: A Domestic Worker Bill of Rights signed in March gives nannies, housekeepers and estate staff minimum wage, overtime and a written agreement from 1 July 2027, and it captures anyone paid for four hours of domestic work in a month.
lead.body:
Washington state's Domestic Worker Bill of Rights was signed into law in March 2026 and takes effect on 1 July 2027. It applies to any hiring entity that pays a person to perform domestic work in a private residence for four or more hours in a month, a threshold low enough to capture the fortnightly housekeeper as well as the full resident household team. The law does not distinguish between a family employing one cleaner and a principal running a staffed estate. Both are employers.

The obligations are the ones a company would recognise. A covered worker must be given a written agreement identifying the position and the rate of pay. Minimum wage and overtime apply. Advance notice of termination is required. The law prohibits conduct that creates an intimidating, hostile or offensive working environment, extends anti-discrimination protection to certain domestic workers and forbids retaliation against a worker who asserts these rights. Enforcement runs through complaints to the Department of Labor and Industries or through private legal action, which means a disputed dismissal in a private house can now end in a state file rather than a quiet settlement.

Washington is not inventing the direction of travel, only accelerating it. Seattle has operated a domestic workers ordinance since 2018. California's Domestic Worker Bill of Rights already extends overtime to certain personal attendants working in the home. At federal level the position has long been unambiguous: household workers are employees rather than independent contractors, they are non-exempt and therefore owed time and a half beyond forty hours in a week, and once cash wages reach USD 3,000 in 2026 the employer must withhold and pay FICA contributions of 15.3 per cent and issue a Form W-2. What changes in Washington is the paperwork, the notice and the exposure.

The operational consequence lands on whoever runs the house. Someone has to hold the written agreements, log the hours of a rota that has traditionally been elastic, record rest breaks, document a termination before it happens and keep the payroll file in a state that survives an inspection. In a single-staff household that person is often the principal's assistant. In a staffed estate it is the house or estate manager, and the role moves further away from hospitality and closer to human resources. Agencies placing staff in Washington will be asked for compliant contract templates well before the 2027 date, because the families who plan properly will want the documents in place a full season early.
lead.why: Private service is moving from private arrangement to documented employment. The professional who can produce a written agreement, an accurate hours record and a clean payroll file is the one a family keeps when the rules tighten.
lead.src: Davis Wright Tremaine, Employment, Labor and Benefits

articles.title: Family offices hold 42 per cent of the portfolio in alternatives, and six in ten intend to move the allocation again within a year
articles.body:
The UBS Global Family Office Report 2026 surveyed 307 family offices with an average family net worth of USD 2.7 billion and average assets under management of USD 1.3 billion. The average portfolio now splits roughly 41 per cent across developed market equities and fixed income, 42 per cent into alternative investments and the remainder into cash and other holdings. Private equity, venture capital and private credit together account for about 29 per cent of the average North American portfolio.

The more striking figure is intent. Sixty per cent of the offices surveyed said they plan to change their strategic asset allocation over the coming twelve months, against 35 per cent who said the same a year earlier. Among those actively making changes, real estate is being trimmed from roughly 11 per cent towards 8 per cent, and private equity from about 21 per cent towards 18 per cent. Capital that used to sit in buildings is moving into credit and into direct stakes in operating companies.

A family that owns less property as an investment does not necessarily own fewer houses. It owns them for a different reason. The residence stops being counted as part of the return and starts being counted as a cost line, which is precisely when household budgets, staffing levels and supplier contracts come under review. Estate managers who can show what a house costs to run, and what each line buys, are arguing from a stronger position than those who cannot.

The shift towards private and direct investment also has a logistical shadow. Direct deals require travel to see the asset, meetings that cannot be delegated and diaries that move at short notice. The households attached to those offices absorb that volatility: more unscheduled flights, more guests to be housed, more principals arriving home at hours that were not on the plan.
articles.why: When property is reclassified from investment to expense, the household budget is examined line by line. Knowing the true annual cost of the house, and being able to defend it, becomes part of the job.

articles.title: Dubai sells 296 homes above USD 10 million in six months, and the prime market pulls away from the rest of the city
articles.body:
Dubai's prime residential sector recorded 296 sales of homes priced above USD 10 million in the first half of 2026, worth a combined USD 5.1 billion, an increase of 14 per cent on the same period a year earlier. The second quarter alone accounted for 131 of those deals. No other city in the world currently clears that many transactions at that level in six months.

The wider market tells a calmer story. The second quarter produced roughly AED 110 billion of sales across about 38,300 transactions, a clear slowdown from the record pace of 2025, with prices rising from 5 to 7 per cent year on year and citywide gross rental yields near 6.6 per cent. Knight Frank has described the result as an increasingly two-speed market, in which prime villa communities continue to outperform while apartment-led districts normalise.

The villa is the point. Buyers at the top of this market are acquiring land, staff accommodation, garages, guest wings and pools rather than lateral apartments, and each of those purchases creates a household rather than a pied-a-terre. Palm Jumeirah, Emirates Hills, Jumeirah Bay and the Dubai Hills villa communities are now home to a permanent, year-round service population rather than a seasonal one.

For the private service market, Dubai has become the counterweight to the European season. Households there run through the summer, when maintenance is at its hardest and staff turnover is highest, and pay accordingly: the Gulf and Monaco sit at the top of international compensation tables for senior household roles. What the emirate still lacks is depth of experienced local candidates, which is why so many senior placements there are made from London, Paris and Geneva.
articles.why: Every USD 10 million villa sold is a household to be staffed, run and maintained in a climate that punishes neglect. Prime sales volume is the closest thing this market has to a hiring forecast.

articles.title: NetJets curtails sales of its jet cards, and access to an aircraft becomes something a family has to secure well in advance
articles.body:
In early August 2026 NetJets limited sales of its jet card and lease products, citing record retention rates among existing customers and surging demand from its own fractional owners. The company is not short of business. It flew 266,500 flights in the first six months of 2026, which amounts to 13.6 per cent of all business jet departures worldwide, and its departures grew 11.8 per cent over the period. Flexjet, the other large fractional operator, grew 11.0 per cent.

The backdrop is a market running well above its historic norm. The global business jet fleet stands at about 24,270 aircraft and flight activity is roughly 32 per cent above pre-pandemic levels. Demand of that order, combined with delivery backlogs at the manufacturers, means the fractional operators can now choose their customers rather than recruit them.

The jet card has been the household's flexible instrument for a decade: a block of hours bought without owning a share, used to cover the weeks when the family's own arrangement did not stretch. Withdrawing it removes the easy overflow option and pushes families back towards fractional shares, which require a longer commitment, or towards the charter market, where August pricing has been unforgiving.

Whoever books the aircraft is therefore doing a different job. It is no longer a matter of calling one provider on the morning of departure. It means holding relationships with several operators, understanding which have availability in which region, knowing the peak day rules and the callout windows inside each contract, and putting requests in earlier than the principal would naturally think to ask.
articles.why: When the flexible product disappears, the value of the person arranging travel shifts from booking to procurement: contracts, alternatives and lead times, held in advance of the request.

articles.title: Monterey sells USD 747.9 million of motor cars in three days, and the garage becomes the fastest moving asset in the house
articles.body:
Five auction houses sold USD 747.9 million of collector cars at Monterey between 13 and 15 August, according to Hagerty's tally. That is 73 per cent above the USD 432.8 million posted over the same days in 2025 and comfortably beyond the previous Monterey record of roughly USD 471 million set in 2022. Pre-sale forecasts had topped out near USD 500 million.

Volume did not drive it. Some 844 of 1,124 lots sold, a sell-through rate of 75 per cent, almost identical to last year. The average price did the work, rising 64 per cent to USD 866,107, and eleven cars made eight figures, more than the previous five Monterey weeks combined. A 1964 Shelby Cobra Daytona Coupe took USD 42,905,000 at Gooding Christie's, a record for any American car. A 2026 Ferrari Luce sold as a charity lot for USD 40 million, a 1996 McLaren F1 GTR made USD 34,655,000, a record for a British car, and a 1963 Corvette Grand Sport reached USD 18,705,000. Ferrari took seven of the ten highest results of the week.

Beneath the headline the market was selective to the point of severity. Only one of the first seventeen prewar cars offered on the Thursday hammered above its low estimate. A 1962 Aston Martin DB4 GT Zagato that made USD 14.3 million in 2015 failed to sell at a bid of USD 11,750,000. A 1936 Mercedes-Benz 500K Roadster went 54 per cent below low estimate. Singular cars with unimpeachable history were fought over. Good but ordinary examples were not.

A collection that reprices this quickly stops being decoration. Insurance schedules, agreed values, storage conditions, transport bookings and maintenance records all have to keep pace, and the person who holds those files is usually inside the household rather than at the auction house. Concours week itself is a logistical operation: enclosed transport booked months ahead, drivers, accommodation in a saturated market and a car that must arrive in a condition worth its estimate.
articles.why: Collections held in the house move in value faster than the house does. Accurate records, correct storage and competent transport are service work, and they carry seven-figure consequences.

articles.title: Singapore refines the conditions attached to family office tax incentives, and the new terms took effect this month
articles.body:
The Monetary Authority of Singapore has refined the economic conditions attached to the tax incentive schemes used by single family office funds, with the changes taking effect from 1 August 2026. The two schemes remain section 13O, the onshore fund exemption, and section 13U, the enhanced-tier exemption.

The thresholds are unchanged in shape. Section 13O requires a minimum of S$20 million in designated investments and at least two investment professionals, of whom at least one is not a family member. Section 13U requires S$50 million and three investment professionals, again with at least one from outside the family. Both carry a capital deployment requirement of the lower of S$10 million or 10 per cent of assets under management into eligible local investments. The refinements raise the assets under management thresholds attached to the higher local business spending tiers and tighten the minimum local spending expected of larger funds, while giving offices more operational flexibility elsewhere.

The scale of what is being regulated is easy to underestimate. More than 2,000 single family offices held these incentives at the end of December 2025, a figure that has grown steadily through the decade and made Singapore the principal Asian base for internationally mobile family capital.

The household follows the office. A family that anchors its structure in Singapore places people there: a principal residence, school places, drivers, a house manager who can operate across time zones and a travel pattern that runs through Hong Kong, Tokyo, Sydney and the Gulf rather than through Europe. Employment terms, work passes and domestic helper regulations in Singapore are precise, and staff are expected to be documented correctly from the first day.
articles.why: Where a family puts its structure determines where it puts its house, and therefore where the jobs are. Reading jurisdiction news is how a candidate anticipates the market rather than following it.

briefs.t: The nanny tax threshold rises to USD 3,000
briefs.b: Cash wages of USD 3,000 or more paid to a household employee during 2026 trigger FICA obligations of 15.3 per cent of wages, up from USD 2,800 in 2025. Any employee paid at or above that level, or from whom federal income tax was withheld, must receive a Form W-2. The threshold now catches part-time and seasonal household staff in most markets.

briefs.t: Private jet departures return to growth
briefs.b: Global business jet departures reached about 78,074 in the first full week of August, the first year on year increase recorded in three weeks. Fractional and charter volumes were broadly flat on the previous week, with growth concentrated in Florida, California and Texas.

briefs.t: 165,000 millionaires expected to move this year
briefs.b: The 2026 edition of the Henley Private Wealth Migration Report projects roughly 165,000 high net worth individuals relocating internationally this year, up from about 142,000 in 2025. That is more than 600 people changing country on every working day, each one a household to be closed, moved or opened.

briefs.t: The estate manager average sits near USD 152,000
briefs.b: Compensation survey data for estate and household roles puts the United States average for an estate manager, including base salary and bonus, at about USD 151,830, with the 75th percentile near USD 181,179. Packages in California and New York run materially above the national figure, and senior multi-property roles in the Gulf and Monaco higher still.
briefs.src: Talent Gurus household staff compensation guide
